q-333779.name: Question 1
q-333779.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)-6y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=x(t)-2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives all equilibrium points of the system of linear differential equations above?
q-333779.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3x-6y=0 \\ x-2y=0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the first equation is a multiple of the second one:

$$
3(x-2y)=3x-6y,
$$

so we can disregard the first equation.

From the second equation, we get

$$
x-2y=0\,⇒\,x=2y.
$$

Therefore, the equilibrium points are given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2k \\ k\end{aligned}],\,k\in R.
$$

q-333782.name: Question 2
q-333782.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4x(t)+2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives all equilibrium points of the system of linear differential equations above?
q-333782.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2x+y=0 \\ 4x+2y=0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the second equation is a multiple of the first one:

$$
2(2x+y)=4x+2y,
$$

so we can disregard the second equation.

From the first equation, we get

$$
2x+y=0\,⇒\,y=-2x.
$$

Therefore, the equilibrium points are given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}k \\ -2k\end{aligned}],\,k\in R.
$$

{x′(t)=2x(t)+y(t)y′(t)=4x(t)+2y(t) Which of the following gives all equilibrium points of the system of linear differential equations above?

a
[x(t)y(t)]=[00] only
b
[x(t)y(t)]=[k−2k],k∈R
c
[x(t)y(t)]=[21] only
d
[x(t)y(t)]=[2k−2k],k∈R
e
[x(t)y(t)]=[k2k],k∈R
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we have x′(t)=[2142]x(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)].

The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system x′(t)=f(x,y) are the points for which f(x,y)=0. So, we get the following system of linear equations: {2x+y=04x+2y=0

Notice that the second equation is a multiple of the first one: 2(2x+y)=4x+2y, so we can disregard the second equation.

From the first equation, we get 2x+y=0⇒y=−2x.

Therefore, the equilibrium points are given by [x(t)y(t)]=[k−2k],k∈R.

q-333832.name: Question 3
q-333832.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)-y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3x(t)+3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}=[1,\text{ }1]^{T}$ and ${v}_{2}=[-1,\text{ }3]^{T},$ respectively. Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the system?

*Hint: Here, the dotted line represents the equilibrium solutions.*
q-333832.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Let's now sketch the phase portrait.

- First, notice that ${x}_{E}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ are the equilibrium solutions of the system since ${x}_{E}^{′}(t)=0.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14130948/assets/18fad31b9f69e55d9f4bc414d3e1b732eaee7685bf36a183033fc302e911eb82.png)

- Now, the line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 
$y=-3x$
and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14130948/assets/2bfda58fee727ccdc9f424140e2b8143bf5afe426ef0b1fa72105272d9a1b41e.png)

All other non-equilibrium solutions are parallel to the vector ${v}_{2}.$ So, the phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

$$

$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ of the system's matrix $A$ is $v=[1,\text{ }3]^{T}.$ The vector $w={[-\frac{1}{3},\text{ }0]}^{T}$ is such that $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$  Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the system?

*Hint: Here, the dotted line represents the equilibrium solutions.*

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =0,\,v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t-\frac{1}{3} \\ 3t\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that ${x}_{E}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ are equilibrium solutions of the system since ${x}_{E}^{′}(t)=0.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=3x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

$$

$$
